passages.t: ‘Save me, O God, by Your name’: when the Ziphites told Saul
passages.happening:
The heading says, “When the Ziphites went to Saul and said, ‘Is David not hiding among us?’” (verse 1). Then the prayer begins. “Save me, O God, by Your name, and vindicate me by Your might!” (verse 1).

The danger is clear. “For strangers rise up against me, and ruthless men seek my life” (verse 3).

The turn comes in the middle. “Surely God is my helper; the Lord is the sustainer of my soul” (verse 4). He asks God to deal with his enemies (verse 5). And he makes a promise. “Freely I will sacrifice to You; I will praise Your name, O LORD, for it is good” (verse 6). The last verse speaks as if the rescue has already come (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Ziph was a town in the hills of Judah. Its people were David's own tribe. Yet they went to Saul to give him away: “Is not David hiding among us in the strongholds at Horesh” (1 Samuel 23:19). Saul nearly caught him, and then had to turn back to fight the Philistines (1 Samuel 23:27-28). It is another heading from David's years on the run, like Psalm 52's.

In the Bible a ‘name’ stands for who someone is. To be saved ‘by Your name’ is to appeal to God's character and promises, the God who told Moses his name.

‘Strangers’ (verse 3) is a strong word for people of his own tribe. Some think the psalm was first written for a different danger and later linked to this story. Others say that people who hand you over to death have made themselves strangers, whatever their family.

A ‘freewill’ offering was not required by any law or vow. It was a gift given only out of thanks.
passages.later: Soon after, David had the chance to kill Saul and would not. He said, “May I never lift my hand against him, since he is the LORD’s anointed” (1 Samuel 24:6). He left judgment to God. Paul gives the same rule to Christians: “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God’s wrath” (Romans 12:19).
passages.asks:
Being betrayed by your own people hurts in a special way. This short psalm moves from fear to trust in seven verses, and its turning point is verse 4: ‘Surely God is my helper.’

The prayer against enemies in verse 5, “In Your faithfulness, destroy them”, is left to God, not acted out. The book page's part on the cursing psalms explains how Christians read prayers like it. And the psalm ends in a gift given freely. Thanks that nobody asked for is a sign of a heart that trusts.
